lessons.title: Understand what AI agents and automations really are — and pick your first one
lessons.summary: Learn the real difference between a classic automation, an AI-in-the-loop workflow, and an autonomous agent, then pick one realistic first automation to build.
lessons.goal: Choose one low-risk, high-frequency task from your own work as your first automation project, using a clear framework instead of guessing.
lessons.whyItMatters: Businesses waste money either automating nothing (everyone stays manual forever) or automating the wrong thing — a flashy 'AI agent' for a task a simple trigger-action tool would handle in ten minutes. Knowing the vocabulary and a simple decision framework lets you spend your first automation project on something that actually saves time, instead of chasing hype.
steps: Define three tiers: classic automation (trigger, then a fixed action, no AI — e.g. 'new form response adds a row to a sheet'), AI-in-the-loop automation (trigger, then an AI does one judgment step like drafting, classifying or summarizing, then an action), and an agent (given a goal, it decides which steps and tools to use, sometimes looping across multiple turns, with real autonomy).

Recognize agent markers: it makes decisions instead of following a fixed script, it calls tools or APIs itself, it can loop (try, check the result, retry), and it usually needs guardrails and human checkpoints because its exact behavior isn't fully predictable in advance.
List five repetitive tasks you or your team do weekly that involve moving information between two or more systems or tools.

For each task, ask whether the bottleneck is AI judgment (writing, deciding, summarizing) or mechanical transfer (copy this into that). Mechanical-only tasks usually need a classic automation, not an agent.

Score each candidate on three criteria: how often it repeats, how much time it costs per instance, and how tolerant the task is of an occasional mistake — a low-stakes internal task is safer to automate first than one touching customers or money.
Pick the single task with the best combination of high frequency, real time cost, and low risk as your first automation, and write it down in one sentence.

Note which kind of tool fits: mechanical-only tasks need a scripted or scheduled trigger-action step; tasks with a judgment step need an AI-in-the-loop workflow such as a ChatGPT scheduled Task, a Claude Cowork delegation, or a Claude Code script. You'll pick the exact tool in later lessons.
lessons.prompt:
I want to pick my first business process to automate with AI. Here are candidate repetitive tasks I do:
[LIST YOUR 5 TASKS, e.g. 1. Forwarding new leads from a contact form into our CRM and writing a personalized first reply. 2. ...]

For each task, tell me:
1. Whether it is mainly mechanical data-transfer, an AI judgment task, or both.
2. A rough estimate of hours per week it costs across the team.
3. The risk level if automation makes a mistake (low/medium/high), and why.
4. Whether it's a good first automation project (yes/no) and why.
Rank the tasks from best to worst first-automation candidate. Do not recommend a specific automation tool yet — just help me prioritize which task to tackle first.
lessons.explanation: The prompt forces the model to separate mechanical work from judgment work, estimate real impact, and weigh risk, instead of just answering 'yes, automate everything.' A good first automation project should be low-risk and high-frequency to build confidence, not the most ambitious task on the list — the ranking step keeps you honest about that.
lessons.example:
Input: five tasks including lead routing, invoice reminders, meeting note summaries, social post drafts, and expense categorization.

Output: a ranked table — e.g. expense categorization ranks first (high frequency, low risk, purely internal), while invoice reminders rank last for a first project because a mistake could confuse a paying customer.
lessons.exercise: In your own AI account (Claude or ChatGPT), list five repetitive tasks from your actual week and run the prompt above. Pick the top-ranked task as your first automation target — you'll build it later in this course.
lessons.expectedResult: You have one clearly named, low-risk, high-frequency task chosen as your first automation project, plus a documented reason why it beats the other four.
commonMistakes: Choosing the most annoying task instead of the most automatable one — annoyance and automatability aren't the same thing.
Jumping straight to 'I need an AI agent' for a task that's pure data transfer with no judgment involved, which just adds cost and failure points.
Picking a task that touches money, legal commitments, or customer-facing communication as the very first automation, before you've built confidence with something lower-stakes.
lessons.proTip: Keep a running list of every task you almost automate — most professionals find their real second and third automation targets while working on the first one.

lessons.title: Map a business process step-by-step before you automate it
lessons.summary: Turn the automation candidate you picked into a precise process map with triggers, decisions, exceptions and a human checkpoint, ready to hand to any automation tool.
lessons.goal: Produce a clean, numbered process map — trigger, systems, steps, exceptions and one human checkpoint — for the automation candidate you chose.
lessons.whyItMatters: The single biggest reason business automations fail isn't the tool — it's an unclear process. If you can't describe exactly what happens today, in what order, with what exceptions, you can't build a reliable automation, and skipping this step means the AI will guess and get it wrong. This mapping method is one you'll reuse for every future automation.
lessons.beforeYouStart: The automation candidate you picked in the previous lesson.
steps: Write the exact trigger event that starts the process today, e.g. 'a new lead fills out our contact form' or 'an invoice becomes 7 days overdue.'
List every system or tool currently touched, in order, e.g. Typeform, then Gmail, then a spreadsheet, then Slack.
List the steps a human currently performs, one action per line, including any decision points such as 'if lead company size is over 50, route to the enterprise rep, otherwise route to the SMB rep.'

Mark which steps are pure data movement, which require a written judgment (drafting, summarizing, classifying), and which require a decision with real consequences, such as approving a refund or sending an external email.
Note every exception or edge case you can think of: missing data, duplicate entries, unusual formats — these are exactly where naive automations break.
Decide the human checkpoint: which step, if any, must a person approve before an action goes out, such as before an email sends to a customer or before a record is deleted.
Feed the process description to an AI to sanity-check for gaps and turn it into a clean numbered flow you can hand to any automation tool.
lessons.prompt:
Here is a business process I want to automate, described in my own words:
[PASTE YOUR TRIGGER, STEPS, SYSTEMS, EXCEPTIONS, AND DESIRED HUMAN CHECKPOINT]

Do the following:
1. Rewrite this as a clean numbered flow: Trigger, then Step 1, Step 2, and so on to the Result, naming the system involved at each step.
2. Flag any step where you can see missing information — data the automation would need but I haven't specified where it comes from.
3. Flag any step that involves subjective judgment (would need AI, not a fixed rule) versus a step that's a fixed rule (would need a simple filter or condition).
4. Point out at least 2 edge cases or exceptions I have not accounted for.
5. Suggest where a human approval checkpoint makes sense, and explain why.
Use only the information I gave you. Do not invent tools, systems, or steps I didn't mention.
lessons.explanation: The structure forces a clean decomposition of trigger, steps and systems, and the anti-hallucination instruction stops the AI from inventing parts of your process it wasn't told about. Separating rule-based steps from judgment steps early matters because that distinction determines which kind of automation tool or node you'll need in later lessons.
lessons.example:
Input: an overdue-invoice-reminder process described loosely.

Output: a numbered flow (Trigger: invoice 7 days overdue → Step 1: check payment status in accounting system → Step 2: draft reminder email → Step 3: send) plus two flagged edge cases — partial payments and disputed invoices — and a suggested checkpoint before any 'final notice' email sends.
lessons.exercise: Take the automation candidate from the previous lesson, write out its current steps in your own words, and run this prompt in your own AI account. Save the cleaned-up flow — you'll build the real automation from it in upcoming lessons.
lessons.expectedResult: A numbered, gap-checked process map with the trigger, each system touched, rule-based versus judgment steps labeled, at least 2 edge cases documented, and one human checkpoint decided.
commonMistakes: Describing the process too vaguely, such as 'customer emails come in, we respond,' instead of naming the actual systems and order of steps — vague input produces a vague, unusable map.
Skipping edge cases because 'they're rare' — rare cases are exactly what breaks unattended automations in production.
Forgetting to decide a human checkpoint at all, which usually means the first mistake the automation makes goes out uncaught.
lessons.proTip: Store this process map as a short doc, even a few bullet points, next to whatever automation you build from it — you'll need it again when something breaks six months from now and nobody remembers why a step exists.

lessons.title: MCP explained: how AI tools actually connect to your other apps
lessons.summary: Understand what the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is, its host-client-server model, and why one connection works the same way across Claude, ChatGPT and other AI tools.
lessons.goal: Explain, in your own words, what MCP is, what a server can expose, and identify one real connector in your own AI tool that matches something you use.
lessons.whyItMatters: Every AI product now talks about 'connectors,' 'integrations,' or 'MCP servers,' and it's easy to click connect without understanding what you're authorizing. Understanding MCP's host, client and server model, and its three primitives — tools, resources and prompts — lets you evaluate what a connector can actually do before you grant it access to your data.
steps: Learn the core idea: MCP is an open standard, introduced by Anthropic in November 2024, for connecting AI applications to outside tools and data using a shared protocol instead of every product building one-off integrations — commonly described as 'USB-C for AI.'

Learn the three roles: the Host is the AI app you're using, such as Claude or ChatGPT; the Client lives inside the host, one per connection; the Server is the external program exposing your tool or data, such as a Notion server, a GitHub server, or a database server.

Learn what a server can expose: Tools are actions the AI can call, like creating a page or running a query; Resources are read-only data the AI can pull into context, like a file or record; Prompts are ready-made message templates the server provides.

Learn the two connection types: local servers that run as a subprocess on your own machine, and remote hosted servers reached over the internet with OAuth login — the far more common pattern in 2026, with official hosted servers from services like GitHub, Notion, Linear, Stripe and Supabase.

Understand why this matters practically: because MCP is a shared standard, connecting one server, say your company's Notion, to Claude also means the same server works, unmodified, in ChatGPT or another MCP-compatible tool — you aren't learning a new integration per AI product.

Understand the access model: connecting a server grants the AI whatever tools and resources that server exposes, scoped by whatever permissions you or your admin approved during OAuth login — not blanket access to everything in your account.
Preview what's next: in the following lesson you'll connect one real MCP connector through your AI tool's built-in connector directory and see this in action.
lessons.prompt:
I use these AI tools: [LIST YOUR AI TOOLS, e.g. Claude, ChatGPT] and these business tools: [LIST YOUR BUSINESS APPS, e.g. Notion, Google Drive, Slack, a Postgres database].

Explain, for my specific combination:
1. Which of my business tools likely already have an official MCP connector or server I could enable directly inside my AI tool's settings, based on what's commonly available in 2026 (Notion, GitHub, Linear, Slack, Google Drive, Stripe and Supabase are common; say clearly if you're not sure about a specific one).
2. In plain language, what granting that connection would let the AI see or do.
3. One question I should ask before connecting each one, such as what data scope it covers or whether it can write and delete, not just read.
Be explicit about uncertainty — if you don't know whether a specific tool has an official connector, say so instead of guessing.
lessons.explanation: The uncertainty instruction is the important part here: connector availability changes constantly, so the prompt is written to make the model flag what it doesn't know rather than confidently invent an integration that may not exist yet.
lessons.example:
Input: 'I use Claude, and Notion plus Google Drive.'

Output: identifies that Notion and Google Drive commonly have official connectors, explains that a Notion connection typically lets the AI read and, depending on scope, create or edit pages, and suggests checking whether the connector can be limited to a specific workspace or folder before connecting.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude or ChatGPT account, open Settings and find Connectors or Integrations, and just browse the list without connecting anything yet — note three tools you recognize from your own stack. Then run the prompt above.
lessons.expectedResult: You can explain the difference between a Host, Client and Server in MCP, name the three things a server can expose, and have identified at least one connector in your own AI tool's settings that matches a tool you actually use.
commonMistakes: Confusing MCP, the protocol, with any single vendor's product — it's used by Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Cursor and many others, not owned by one company.
Assuming 'connected' means full account access — a server only exposes the specific tools and resources it was built to expose, and OAuth scopes further limit that.

Treating local and remote servers as the same risk profile — a local server runs with your machine's own permissions, while a remote one runs on someone else's infrastructure under whatever access you grant it.
lessons.proTip: When evaluating a new MCP server, look for its list of exposed tools before connecting — most connector directories show tool names such as 'create_page' or 'search_records,' so you know exactly what actions the AI could take, not just what data it could read.

lessons.title: Connect your first MCP connector safely
lessons.summary: Enable one real MCP connector in your Claude or ChatGPT account with a minimal-risk scope, and verify it works with a safe, read-only test before trusting it further.
lessons.goal: Connect one MCP connector with the narrowest available permission scope and confirm it works correctly with a read-only verification test.
lessons.whyItMatters: This is where MCP stops being theory. Doing this once carefully — checking scopes, starting read-only, testing before trusting — builds the habit you need before connecting anything higher-stakes, like a CRM, a billing system, or a shared email account.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A Claude or ChatGPT account, and one tool you already use that has a known connector, such as Google Drive, Notion, GitHub or Slack. Pick a tool where a mistake would be low-consequence for this first test.
steps: Open your AI tool's connector or integration settings — in Claude, Settings then Connectors; in ChatGPT, Settings then Connectors — and find the service you chose.

Before clicking connect, read what the connector page says it can do: look for whether it lists specific tools or actions such as read files, create pages, or send messages, and whether read and write are separate toggles.
Start with the narrowest scope offered — if there's a choice between read-only and read/write, or between a single folder and the entire account, pick the narrower option for your first connection.
Complete the OAuth login flow in the popup window, and confirm you're logging into the correct account, especially if you have multiple accounts for the same service such as personal versus work.
Once connected, run one safe, read-only test in a new chat: ask the AI to find and summarize one specific, non-sensitive item from the connected service.
Check the response against reality: did it find the right item, and did it only read rather than modify anything?

If the connector supports write actions you plan to use later, deliberately test one low-stakes write action next, such as creating a test page or note, so you see exactly what 'the AI takes an action' looks like before automating anything real.
Write down what you connected, what scope you granted, and the date — you'll want this record when you eventually audit or revoke connectors.
lessons.prompt:
You're connected to my [SERVICE NAME, e.g. Notion] account through this chat.

Find [SPECIFIC ITEM, e.g. the most recent page in my Marketing section] and give me:
1. Its title and last-edited date.
2. A 3-sentence summary of its content.
3. A direct link if one is available.
Do not create, edit, or delete anything — this is a read-only check. If you are unable to find it, tell me exactly what you searched for instead of guessing at an answer.
lessons.explanation: The prompt explicitly forbids write actions during the verification step and instructs honesty over guessing when the search fails, which matters most while you're still building trust in a brand-new connection and want to isolate whether any problem is the connector, the AI, or your instructions.
lessons.example: Connecting Google Drive, then asking 'find my most recent doc in the Q3 Planning folder and summarize it' returns the title, last-edited date, a 3-sentence summary, and a link, with no edits made to the file.
lessons.exercise: In your own Claude or ChatGPT account, connect one real MCP connector for a tool you use, using the narrowest scope available, then run the read-only test prompt above.
lessons.expectedResult: You have one working MCP connector, granted the minimum scope needed, verified with a read-only test that returned accurate information without taking any unintended action, and a short written record of what you connected and when.
commonMistakes: Granting full read/write account access by default because it's the pre-selected option, instead of checking for a narrower scope.
Skipping the verification step and immediately trying a complex multi-step task, so if something goes wrong you can't tell whether the connector, the AI, or your instructions caused it.
Never revisiting connected services later — connectors should be reviewed and pruned periodically, not connected once and forgotten.
lessons.proTip: Keep a simple list, even a plain note file, of every connector you've approved across every AI tool, with the date and scope — most people lose track after the third or fourth one, which is exactly how stale, over-permissioned connections pile up.

lessons.title: Build a ChatGPT scheduled Task that handles a recurring judgment call
lessons.summary: Set up a ChatGPT Task that runs on a schedule, applies a judgment rule to new information, and delivers a correctly formatted output every time — a recurring automation built natively inside ChatGPT.
lessons.goal: Ship a live, tested ChatGPT Task whose recurring judgment rule produces a correctly formatted, ready-to-use output on schedule.
lessons.whyItMatters: Dedicated automation platforms like Zapier, Make, and n8n pioneered the trigger-then-judgment-then-action pattern for exactly this kind of recurring task. ChatGPT's Tasks feature brings the same pattern natively into a tool you already use — no separate platform, login, or per-task billing to manage for a lightweight recurring job.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A ChatGPT Plus account or higher (Tasks requires a paid plan), and the process map you built earlier in this course — ideally one with a clear recurring trigger and one AI judgment step.
steps: If the judgment step needs the same standing rules and context every run, build it as a Custom GPT first: Explore GPTs → Create → write system instructions containing your judgment rules, so the schedule reuses that exact configured behavior.
In the ChatGPT composer, open the tools menu and choose Tasks (or simply ask ChatGPT to 'create a scheduled task' for this) to open the scheduling flow.

Write the task's standing instructions the same way you'd write any AI judgment step: state the exact decision to make, reference the real source of the information — an uploaded file, a connected service such as Gmail if you've enabled that connector, or data you'll paste in each run — and define the exact output format you need.
Set the schedule, daily, weekly, or a specific recurring time, matching how often the real-world trigger actually happens; don't schedule hourly for something that only changes once a week.

Add explicit constraints to the instructions: what to do if there's nothing new to process that run, and what to do if required information is missing or ambiguous — a scheduled task with no one watching it needs the same missing-data fallback any other automation does.
Run the task immediately with Run Now instead of waiting for the schedule, and read the full output, not just skim it, to confirm it followed your judgment rule correctly.
Adjust the instructions if the output format or judgment was off, then run it again on a second, different real example before trusting the schedule.
Let the task run on its schedule for the first several cycles, checking ChatGPT's task history each time, before considering it set and forget.
lessons.prompt:
Every [FREQUENCY, e.g. weekday morning at 8am], review the leads I paste into this task and classify each one as Enterprise or SMB.
Rules: company size over 50 employees is Enterprise. 50 or fewer is SMB. If company size is missing or not a number, mark it UNKNOWN.
If there is nothing new to process this run, reply exactly: Nothing new today.
Otherwise reply with a short table: one row per lead, columns Name, Company, Size, Classification. Do not add commentary outside the table.
lessons.explanation: The instructions define an explicit decision rule rather than leaving it to the model's judgment alone, force a constrained table format so you can scan the result in seconds, and specify both a missing-data fallback and a nothing-to-report fallback so an unattended scheduled run never silently guesses or goes quiet.
lessons.example: A Task scheduled for 8am each weekday receives a pasted batch of new leads and returns a table with Enterprise/SMB classifications for review; on a morning with no new leads, it replies 'Nothing new today' instead of inventing a row.
lessons.exercise: Build this Task in your own ChatGPT account using the low-risk recurring automation you mapped earlier in this course. Run it once with Run Now against real data before trusting the schedule.
lessons.expectedResult: A live, scheduled ChatGPT Task with a working judgment rule whose output is correctly formatted every run, verified against at least one real Run Now test with actual data, not a hypothetical example.
commonMistakes: Writing the task's instructions around a single hypothetical example instead of the real, messy input it will actually see each run, so the first live run behaves differently than the test.
Leaving the output format open-ended when you need a specific value or shape to act on, which makes the recurring output inconsistent from run to run.
Turning on the schedule without running it manually against real data first, and without checking whether it handles the 'nothing new' case correctly.
lessons.proTip: Check ChatGPT's task history after a run misbehaves — you can see exactly what instructions and context that run used and fix the standing instructions before the next scheduled run, without waiting for the next real trigger.

lessons.title: Script a branching automation with Claude Code for more control
lessons.summary: Use Claude Code's headless mode to script a branching workflow where an AI judgment step produces structured output that correctly routes execution down different paths — for a process that needs more control than a single scheduled task offers.
lessons.goal: Write and run a small script, driven by Claude Code's headless mode, where an AI step produces structured JSON output that correctly routes execution down at least two different paths.
lessons.whyItMatters: A single scheduled task is fast to set up, but once a process needs real branching — different actions for different outcomes, retries, or chaining multiple AI calls — a short script gives you far more control than a chat-based tool alone. Claude Code's headless mode (`claude -p`) lets you call Claude from a plain script, and its hooks let you enforce rules deterministically around it, which is exactly the control a growing automation needs.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Claude Code installed and signed in (`npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`, then run `claude` once interactively to log in), basic comfort running a shell script, and a process from your map that has at least one branch or condition, not just a straight line.
steps: Write a small input source that represents your trigger — for example a text file with one support message per line, or a short script that pulls new rows from wherever your data lives.

Write the branching logic in plain shell, or a short Python or Node script: for each input item, call Claude Code headlessly with `claude -p "<your instructions>" --output-format json`, substituting the item's real content into the prompt.

Write the AI step's instructions with the same discipline as any judgment step: reference the real input content directly, state the exact structured output format you need, in this case valid JSON with a category field, and define a fallback for missing or ambiguous input.

Parse the returned JSON's category field in your script, then branch: route each category to a different action, such as appending to a different log file, calling a webhook, or printing an alert — this is your router, done in code instead of a visual branch node.

Add a Claude Code hook, or a simple check inside the script itself, that blocks any risky follow-on action, such as actually sending an email or calling a paid API, from firing automatically, and logs it for a human to review instead — the scripted equivalent of an approval checkpoint.
Run the script against at least two different sample inputs, including one edge case from your process map, and inspect the AI step's raw JSON output for each one, not just where it got routed.
Fix any case where the AI's output didn't match your required JSON shape or picked the wrong category, tightening the instructions until both test cases behave correctly.

Wire the script to run on a trigger you control — a cron job, a Claude Code hook on a file-watch event, or simply running it manually each morning — and check its log output for the first several real runs before trusting it unattended.
lessons.prompt:
You are triaging inbound support messages for [BUSINESS NAME].
Message: [PASTE THE REAL MESSAGE TEXT HERE]
Customer tier: [PASTE THE REAL CUSTOMER TIER HERE]

Classify this message into exactly one category: Billing, Technical, General, or Urgent-Escalation.
Use Urgent-Escalation only if the message mentions a complete outage, a security issue, or the customer explicitly threatens to cancel.
Respond with valid JSON only, in this exact shape: {"category": "...", "one_line_reason": "..."}
Do not include any text outside the JSON object.
lessons.explanation: Forcing structured JSON output makes the result directly parseable by your script's branching logic, instead of scraping a free-text sentence. The tight category definition, with an explicit trigger condition for the highest-stakes category, reduces false positives and negatives on the branch that matters most, and substituting the real message directly into the prompt keeps each headless call grounded in real input rather than a template variable that was never filled in.
lessons.example: A script reads a support inbox export and substitutes each message into the prompt above, piping it to `claude -p ... --output-format json`. A message reading 'the whole dashboard is down for our whole team' returns {"category": "Urgent-Escalation", "one_line_reason": "Customer reports complete outage"}, and the script's branch logic appends it to urgent.log and calls a webhook that pings the on-call Slack channel, instead of the routine daily-digest.log every other message goes to.
lessons.exercise: Rebuild the branching automation from your process map as a small script driven by `claude -p`, with at least one branch based on the AI step's structured output. Test with two inputs, one of which should trigger the branch.
lessons.expectedResult: A working script where a headless Claude Code call produces structured, parseable JSON output, at least one branch that correctly routes based on that output, and two successful test runs with logged output — one that should trigger the branch, one that shouldn't.
commonMistakes: Asking for free-text output when the script needs to branch on it — always require valid JSON with a specific field name when your script's logic depends on parsing the result.
Skipping the hook or check that blocks risky follow-on actions, so a bad classification can trigger a real send or spend automatically instead of logging for review.
Not testing the edge case that should hit the rare branch, since running the script once with typical input leaves the risky branch unverified until it happens for real.
lessons.proTip: Run `claude -p` with `--output-format json`, not the default text output, whenever a script needs to parse the result — it wraps the response in a structured envelope your script can reliably read instead of scraping free text.

lessons.title: Design agent instructions that are safe and reliable
lessons.summary: Write standing instructions for an AI agent that constrain its tool access, define hard boundaries, and specify how it should behave when uncertain.
lessons.goal: Produce a red-teamed, revised instruction set for a real agent that gates its risky tool access behind explicit rules and a clear ask-instead-of-guess default.
lessons.whyItMatters: An agent with tool access — one that can send emails, modify records, spend money, or post publicly — is only as safe as its instructions. Vague instructions like 'handle customer emails' invite the agent to take actions you never intended. Well-designed instructions are the actual safety mechanism for most real-world agent deployments, not a separate technical safeguard bolted on afterward.
lessons.beforeYouStart: An agent or automated assistant, built as a Claude Cowork delegation, a ChatGPT Custom GPT, or a Claude Code subagent, that has or will have access to at least one real tool or action, not just a read-only task.
steps: Write the agent's single, specific job in one sentence — the narrower the better, since 'draft replies to billing questions' is safer and more debuggable than 'handle customer support.'

List every tool or action the agent actually has access to, and explicitly separate them into two groups: safe to run automatically, such as reading data or drafting a message for review, and requires human approval, such as sending an external email, issuing a refund, deleting a record, or posting publicly.

Write explicit boundaries: name specific actions the agent must never take regardless of what it decides mid-task, such as never issuing a refund over a set amount, never contacting a customer outside business hours, or never modifying pricing.

Define its behavior under uncertainty: what should it do if required information is missing, contradictory, or the task doesn't match any case you anticipated — the default should be pause and ask a human, not make a reasonable guess and proceed.

Give it a small number of worked examples, two to four, showing correct behavior on both a normal case and an edge case, since concrete examples constrain behavior far more reliably than abstract rules alone.
Specify exactly what output or action confirms success, so downstream steps, and you when reviewing logs, can tell a correct run from a silently wrong one.
Have a second AI, or a colleague, red-team the instructions: ask it to find a case where an agent following these exact instructions could still cause harm or take an unintended action.
Revise the instructions to close the gaps the red-team pass found, then version and date the instructions file so you can track changes over time.
lessons.prompt:
Here are draft standing instructions for an AI agent I'm deploying:
[PASTE YOUR DRAFT INSTRUCTIONS]

This agent has access to these tools: [LIST TOOLS, e.g. read customer records, draft email replies, send email, update order status].

Act as a skeptical reviewer. Find:
1. Any instruction that is ambiguous enough that two reasonable people could interpret it differently.
2. Any tool access that isn't explicitly constrained by a rule in these instructions, meaning the agent could technically use it in a way I haven't addressed.
3. At least one realistic scenario where an agent following these instructions literally would take an action I probably don't want.
4. Whether the 'what to do when uncertain' behavior is clearly defined, or whether the agent would have to guess.
Be specific — cite the exact instruction text you're flagging for each issue, not general commentary.
lessons.explanation: This is a red-teaming prompt, not a drafting prompt — it asks the model to actively hunt for gaps and cite specific text, which surfaces real weaknesses far more effectively than asking it to generically 'review this and improve it.'
lessons.example: Draft instructions say 'respond to customer emails professionally.' The red-team pass flags: no constraint on the send action, so the agent could send external emails with no human check; no defined behavior for angry or legal-threat emails; no boundary on discussing pricing or making promises.
lessons.exercise: Write standing instructions for a real agent you're building or already run, then paste them into your own AI account with the red-team prompt above. Revise based on at least two of the gaps it finds.
lessons.expectedResult: A revised, dated instruction set with unsafe or unconstrained tool access explicitly gated to human approval, a clear ask-instead-of-guess rule for uncertain cases, at least two worked examples, and documented resolution of the gaps the red-team pass surfaced.
commonMistakes: Writing instructions around the happy path only, with no rule for missing data, contradictions, or requests outside scope, since agents default to improvising exactly where you didn't specify.

Granting an agent a powerful action, such as send, delete, pay, or post, without a hard rule constraining it, on the assumption that it will use good judgment — good judgment is not a substitute for an explicit boundary.
Treating the instructions as done after the first draft instead of red-teaming them, since the gaps are rarely visible to the person who wrote the instructions in the first place.
lessons.proTip: Keep the 'never do X' boundaries as a short, separate, clearly labeled list at the top of the instructions rather than buried in prose — agents, and humans reviewing the instructions later, follow hard constraints more reliably when they're structurally distinct from general guidance.

lessons.title: Build human-in-the-loop checkpoints and error handling into your automations
lessons.summary: Add explicit approval checkpoints and error-handling paths to an existing automation so failures get caught and routed to a human instead of failing silently.
lessons.goal: Add at least one human approval checkpoint and one explicit, tested error path to a real automation you've already built.
lessons.whyItMatters: The gap between a demo automation and a production-safe one is almost always error handling. A workflow that works perfectly in testing will eventually hit an API timeout, malformed data, or a case the AI step didn't handle correctly — the difference between a minor blip and a real problem is whether that failure gets caught and routed to a human, or silently proceeds.
lessons.beforeYouStart: A working automation from an earlier lesson in this course, built as a ChatGPT Task or a Claude Code script, that currently has no explicit approval step or error path.
steps: Identify every action step in your automation that is hard to reverse or customer- or money-facing, such as sending an external message, charging a card, deleting a record, or posting publicly — these are your checkpoint candidates.

For each checkpoint candidate, add an explicit approval step before the action: in a ChatGPT Task, instruct it to draft the action and post it to you for confirmation rather than executing directly — ChatGPT's agent mode already pauses at sensitive steps like logins and payments by design; in a Claude Code script, add a Claude Code hook, or a simple confirmation check in the script, that blocks the risky action and instead sends the proposed action to a Slack channel or email for a human to approve before it runs.
Design the approval message itself to include everything the reviewer needs to decide quickly without opening another tool: what triggered this, what the AI decided, and the proposed action in full.

Add explicit error handling on every step that calls an external API or AI model: in a script, wrap the call in a try/catch, or check the exit code of `claude -p`, so a failure sends an alert instead of stalling silently; in a ChatGPT Task, add an instruction for what the task should report if a connected service or search fails, so a failed run still tells you it failed instead of going quiet.

Define a fallback for AI steps specifically: if the AI's output doesn't match the expected format, such as not valid JSON or not one of the allowed categories, route to a needs-human-review path instead of letting a malformed value flow into the next step.
Add a timeout or retry policy on steps that call slow or occasionally flaky services, with a cap on retries so a broken dependency doesn't loop forever or spam the same alert repeatedly.

Test the error paths deliberately: temporarily break a step with bad credentials or malformed test input, and confirm the alert or approval path fires correctly instead of just re-testing the happy path again.

Document, next to the automation, who is responsible for responding to approval requests and error alerts, and what the expected response time is — an approval checkpoint nobody monitors is worse than no checkpoint.
lessons.prompt:
I'm adding error handling to this automation step: [DESCRIBE THE STEP, e.g. an AI step that classifies a support ticket and a following step that sends an automated reply email].

Help me design:
1. What exact conditions should trigger a 'needs human review' path instead of letting the automation continue — list specific failure modes such as malformed AI output, a missing required field, or a low-confidence classification.
2. What information the human reviewer needs in the alert or approval message to decide quickly without checking another system.
3. A reasonable retry policy for the external API calls in this step: how many retries, what backoff, and when to give up and alert instead of retrying.
Be specific to the step I described — don't give generic error-handling advice that doesn't reference the actual failure modes of this step.
lessons.explanation: The prompt asks for failure modes specific to the actual step rather than generic advice, and separates three distinct concerns — when to escalate to a human, what the escalation should contain, and the retry policy for transient failures — that are easy to conflate but need different designs.
lessons.example: For an AI classification step, the identified failure modes are: output isn't valid JSON, category isn't one of the four allowed values, or a phrase like 'I'm not sure' appears in the output. All three route to a Slack alert with the raw message and AI output attached, tagged for human review.
lessons.exercise: Take one automation you've already built in this course and add at least one approval checkpoint and one explicit error path, following the design questions above. Break the step on purpose to confirm the alert fires.
lessons.expectedResult: The automation now has at least one human approval checkpoint on a consequential action, an explicit error path with a defined retry policy, and you've confirmed by deliberately breaking a step that the alert or approval request actually fires as designed.
commonMistakes: Building the approval checkpoint but never assigning or monitoring who responds to it, so it becomes a silent backlog instead of a safety net.
Only testing the happy path, so an error path exists on paper but has never actually fired and might be broken.
Retrying failed steps indefinitely without a cap, which can spam alerts or downstream systems, such as sending the same email multiple times, when a dependency is down.
lessons.proTip: Route approval requests and error alerts to a channel or inbox that's actually checked daily, not a rarely opened one created specifically for this automation — the checkpoint is only as good as someone seeing it in time.

lessons.title: Chain a cross-tool pipeline: research, draft, and publish automatically
lessons.summary: Connect a research step, an AI drafting step, and a publish or notify step into one end-to-end pipeline across multiple tools, with a human review point before anything goes live.
lessons.goal: Build and run, end to end, a three-stage pipeline where a drafting step is grounded only in its own research stage's findings, landing in front of a human before anything publishes.
lessons.whyItMatters: Real business value from automation usually comes from chaining tools together, not from any single AI call. A pipeline that researches a topic, drafts content or a report from it, and gets it in front of the right reviewer or system automatically turns a half-day task into minutes of human review — a pattern that generalizes across content marketing, sales research, and operational reporting.
lessons.beforeYouStart: Claude Code installed and signed in, a Claude or ChatGPT account with web search enabled for the research stage, and wherever you publish, such as a CMS, Notion, Slack, or email, ideally reachable through an MCP server or a simple API call.
steps: Define the three stages explicitly: what triggers research, such as a topic list, a schedule, or a new item in a queue; what the draft stage needs to produce and in what format; and where the final output needs to land for human review, such as a CMS draft, a Slack message, or a shared doc.
Set the trigger for your script: a cron job, a Claude Code hook on a file-watch event, or simply a topic you pass as an argument each time you run it, that kicks off the research stage.

Wire the research step: call Claude with web search enabled, either in a chat or via `claude -p`, with a tightly scoped brief — the exact topic, the audience, what sources or scope to prioritize, and what to exclude.
Capture the research output in a structured form, such as bullet findings with sources, so the next stage has clean, sourced input rather than one long undifferentiated block of text.

Wire the drafting step: feed the structured research into a second AI call, either a fresh `claude -p` invocation or a follow-up chat turn, with instructions on format, length, and tone, and, critically, an instruction to only use facts from the supplied research and flag anything it's unsure about rather than inventing supporting detail.

Wire the publish or notify step: send the draft to a review surface a human actually checks, using an MCP server connection such as a Notion or Slack MCP server, or a simple API call — never wire the pipeline to publish or send externally without a human step first.

Add the human decision point explicitly: approve and publish, request revisions that loop back to the drafting step with feedback, or reject — using the same approval-checkpoint pattern from the previous lesson.
Run the full pipeline end to end on one real topic, checking each stage's output individually, not just the final draft, before trusting the whole chain, then schedule or trigger it for ongoing use.
lessons.prompt:
Using only the research findings below, draft a [CONTENT TYPE, e.g. 600-word blog post section] for [AUDIENCE].

Research findings:
[PASTE STRUCTURED RESEARCH OUTPUT FROM THE PREVIOUS STAGE]

Rules:
- Use only facts contained in the research findings above. Do not invent statistics, quotes, or claims not present in the findings.
- If the research findings don't cover something needed for a complete draft, write [NEEDS RESEARCH: topic] inline instead of filling the gap yourself.
- Match this tone: [DESCRIBE TONE, e.g. direct, practical, no hype].
- End with a short list of the source references from the findings that support the main claims.
lessons.explanation: The anti-hallucination constraint is essential once research and drafting are separate automated stages, because a drafting step with no access to real-time verification will otherwise fill gaps with plausible-sounding invented content. The inline gap-flagging instruction turns a silent failure into a visible one a human reviewer can catch.
lessons.example: A topic queue entry reading 'AI adoption in small accounting firms' produces 6 sourced research bullets. The drafting stage writes a 600-word section citing those findings, with one [NEEDS RESEARCH: pricing data] flag where the research didn't cover cost, and a Slack message goes to the content lead with the draft and the flag visible for review.
lessons.exercise: Build a three-stage pipeline, research, draft, human review, for one real recurring content or reporting need in your work, using the tools you have access to. Run it once end to end on a real topic and review each stage's raw output.
lessons.expectedResult: A working pipeline that produces a draft grounded only in its own research stage's findings, with any real gaps flagged inline rather than invented, landing in a review surface a human actually checks before anything publishes or sends externally.
commonMistakes: Skipping the human review stage and wiring the pipeline straight to publish, on the assumption the drafting step's anti-hallucination instructions are a sufficient safeguard on their own — they reduce but don't eliminate errors.
Letting the drafting stage's prompt omit the 'use only supplied research' constraint, which lets it blend real research with invented-sounding filler that's hard to tell apart on a quick read.
Not inspecting the research stage's raw output before trusting the draft — if the research stage returns thin or off-topic findings, the draft will look polished but be built on weak material.
lessons.proTip: Log the raw output of every stage, research findings, draft, and reviewer decision, somewhere searchable, even just a spreadsheet row per run — when a published piece turns out to have an error, you need to trace back through which stage introduced it.

lessons.title: Evaluate and maintain your automations before they quietly break
lessons.summary: Set up a lightweight, recurring review process that catches automation drift, cost creep, and silent failures before they cause real damage.
lessons.goal: Build a written inventory of your live automations with owners and review cadence, and run one real diagnostic pass on an automation's run history.
lessons.whyItMatters: Automations don't fail loudly most of the time — they fail quietly: an API changes its response format, an MCP connector's token expires, a model update changes output style just enough to break a downstream parser, or usage creeps past what your plan's session window comfortably covers as volume grows. Without a maintenance habit, the automations you built in this course become exactly the kind of unmonitored risk this course taught you to avoid.
lessons.beforeYouStart: At least one live automation from earlier in this course, ideally one that's been running for a while.
steps: List every live automation you or your team run, across ChatGPT Tasks, Claude Cowork delegations, and Claude Code scripts, in one place — most people are surprised how many they've accumulated once they actually list them.

For each one, record what triggers it, what it costs — a chunk of your Claude or ChatGPT plan's usage window, Claude Code API spend visible with `/cost`, or a Task's run count — who owns it, and when it was last reviewed.
Set a recurring review cadence based on stakes: weekly for anything customer-facing or money-touching, monthly for internal-only automations, and put it on an actual calendar, not a mental note.

At each review, check the run history and logs for error rates, not just whether it's still running — a spike in the error-path or approval-rejection rate is an early warning sign worth investigating even if nothing crashed.

Spot-check actual outputs against reality periodically, not just error logs, since an AI step can produce technically valid but subtly wrong output, such as a bad classification or a drifted tone, that never trips an error path.

Check MCP server connections and any connected accounts for expired OAuth tokens, revoked access, or upcoming deprecations — Anthropic and OpenAI both announce model and API changes, so read the changelog for anything the automation depends on before it breaks unexpectedly.

Track cost against the value it's delivering — if a scripted automation's API spend or a scheduled task's usage has grown, recheck whether it still fits comfortably inside your plan's usage window, or whether it's time to move it to a cheaper approach.
Retire or consolidate automations that no longer match a real, current need — an old automation still running for a process that changed is actively harmful, not just wasteful.
lessons.prompt:
Here is the run and error log summary for one of my automations over the last [TIME PERIOD]:
[PASTE OR DESCRIBE: number of runs, number of errors, number of human-review escalations, any error messages you've seen repeated]

Analyze this and tell me:
1. Is the error or escalation rate concerning relative to total runs, and why or why not.
2. Based on the error messages I've included, what's the most likely root cause category, such as a data format change, an expired credential, a rate limit, or AI output drift — flag if you don't have enough information to tell, rather than guessing a specific cause.
3. What I should check first to confirm the root cause.
4. Whether this looks like a one-off or a pattern I should watch over more reviews.
Base your analysis only on the data I've given you.
lessons.explanation: This is a diagnostic prompt for an ongoing maintenance habit, not a one-time build prompt — it asks the model to reason about a rate rather than a single incident, explicitly separate root-cause categories, and be honest when the log data isn't sufficient to pinpoint a cause, which matters because guessing wrong here wastes real debugging time.
lessons.example: A log summary of '140 runs, 6 errors, all with the message invalid_grant' produces a diagnosis that the pattern strongly suggests an expired or revoked OAuth token on one connected MCP server rather than a data or rate-limit issue, and recommends checking connector status in the platform's settings first.
lessons.exercise: Pull the run history for one automation you've built during this course, however small, and run this diagnostic prompt against a real summary of its recent runs, even if it currently shows zero errors — this is the habit to build before it doesn't.
lessons.expectedResult: You have a written inventory of your live automations with owner, cost, and last-reviewed noted, a recurring review cadence scheduled, and you've run at least one real diagnostic pass on an automation's actual run history.
commonMistakes: Treating 'it's still running' as equivalent to 'it's still working correctly' — an automation can run without erroring while quietly producing wrong output.
Never checking connected account or token status until an automation stops completely, instead of catching an expiring connection during a scheduled review.
Letting automations accumulate with no single owner responsible for reviewing each one — an automation everyone assumes someone else is watching is an automation nobody is watching.
lessons.proTip: When Anthropic or OpenAI announces a model or API change, search your own automations for anything depending on that specific model or endpoint before the change ships — most breakage from provider updates is entirely predictable in advance if you're subscribed to the right changelog.
